summary.text: A quantum state is a mathematical entity that represents a physical system, and knowing it, plus the rules for how it changes in time, tells you everything that can be known about the system.
Unlike a classical state, such as a cannonball's position and velocity, a quantum state is made of complex numbers and only predicts probabilities for measurement outcomes.
Measuring a quantum system samples from those probabilities, and measurements that are incompatible with each other alter the state.

facts.label: Two types
facts.value: Quantum states are either pure or mixed

facts.label: Pure state form
facts.value: Commonly written as a vector in a Hilbert space

facts.label: Mixed state form
facts.value: Statistical mixtures, commonly written as density matrices

facts.label: Classical comparison
facts.value: A cannonball's state is its position and velocity

facts.label: Examples
facts.value: Wave functions, spin vectors, and many-body states in Fock space

items.prompt: You know a cannon's position and the speed of its shots. How is predicting a cannonball different from predicting an electron's state?

options.label: Both can be predicted exactly in the same way
The cannonball only has a probability of landing anywhere
The cannonball's path can be predicted precisely, but the electron gives only probabilities
The electron's path is always more precise than a cannonball's

items.explain: A classical state evolves under equations of motion and stays strictly determined. Quantum states provide only a probability distribution for outcomes.

items.prompt: A physicist fires many identical electrons at a double slit and records where each one lands. What does the quantum state predict?

options.label: The exact landing spot of each individual electron
The probability distribution of counts across the detector
That every electron lands at the center
Nothing at all, since the state is only decoration

items.explain: The state consists of complex values over the detection region and, when squared, predicts the probability distribution of electron counts.

items.prompt: After measuring a particle's momentum several times, you get the same value each time. Then you measure its position. What happens to the next momentum reading?

options.label: It may differ, since the position measurement altered the state
It stays the same, since momentum cannot change
It always becomes zero after a position check
It can no longer be measured at all

items.explain: Momentum and position are incompatible measurements, and the quantum state appears unavoidably altered by incompatible measurements.

items.prompt: What does repeating an identical measurement over and over on a prepared quantum state tend to show?

options.label: A random value each time, with no pattern
A value that fades as you keep measuring
A different set of values each day
Consistent values, which is why measurements prepare states

items.explain: Whatever the input state, repeated identical measurements give consistent values, so measurements place the system in a partially defined state.

items.prompt: A lab needs to describe a system that is a statistical blend of several different pure states. How is it usually written down?

options.label: As a density matrix
As a single vector in Hilbert space
As a cannonball trajectory
As one real number

items.explain: Mixed states are statistical mixtures of pure states and cannot be represented as vectors; they are commonly represented as density matrices.

items.prompt: In classical mechanics you measure one body once, then check the prediction. How does testing a quantum prediction differ?

options.label: A single measurement is enough to confirm it
Many repeated measurements are compared with predicted probabilities
No measurement is ever compared with predictions
Only the final state matters, never the starting one

items.explain: In quantum mechanics, ensembles of identically prepared states evolve, and many repeated measurements are compared with predicted probability distributions.

beats.title: Everything You Can Know
beats.hook: A cannonball's future is fixed by two numbers, but an electron's comes with dice.

beats.prompt: You know a cannon's position and its shot speed exactly. Gravity is the only force. What can you predict about the cannonball's path?
beats.explain: A classical state evolves under equations of motion and stays strictly determined, so the trajectory can be predicted precisely. A quantum state only gives a probability distribution for outcomes.

choices.label: Only odds of where it might land
choices.feedback: That is how quantum states work; classical states remain strictly determined.

choices.label: Nothing until it lands
choices.feedback: Equations of motion let you predict ahead of time.

beats.prompt: Sort each description into classical or quantum state.

left.label: Position and velocity with well-defined real values
Complex numbers that give only probabilities
Evolves under equations of motion and stays strictly determined

beats.explain: Classical variables have definite real values; quantum values are complex, quantized, limited by uncertainty and give only probabilities.

beats.prompt: Put the steps of describing a quantum system in order.

items.label: Identify the variables that define the state
Measure a compatible set to prepare a unique state
The state evolves by the equations of motion
A later measurement samples from the predicted probabilities

beats.explain: You choose variables, prepare the state, let it evolve deterministically, and measuring then yields one sample from a probability distribution.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: I measure a particle's momentum along x, and get the same value every time I repeat it.
Then I measure its position once.
Position and momentum are incompatible, so the state is altered.
So my next momentum reading must still equal the earlier one.

beats.explain: An incompatible measurement alters the state, so later momentum readings are no longer guaranteed to match.

beats.idea: A quantum state holds all that can be known about a system, but it predicts only probabilities, and some measurements change it.

paragraphs.heading: Everything that can be known
paragraphs.text: In quantum physics, a quantum state is a piece of mathematics that stands for a physical system. Quantum mechanics sets the rules for building a state, for how it changes, and for measuring it. If you know the state and the rules for how the system changes over time, you know all there is to know about it.

paragraphs.heading: From cannonballs to electrons
paragraphs.text: The idea grew out of states in classical mechanics. A classical state is a set of quantities with definite real values at each moment; a cannonball's state is its position and velocity. These values follow equations of motion, so with gravity in the equations you can predict the ball's path exactly. Quantum states also hold variables that follow equations of motion. But their values are complex numbers, come only in set steps, are limited by uncertainty relations, and give only probabilities for outcomes.

paragraphs.heading: An electron at two slits
paragraphs.text: In the double-slit experiment, for example, an electron's quantum state is a set of complex values across the detection area. Squared, those values predict only the probability pattern of electron counts across the detector. Because measurement in quantum physics is a matter of chance, quantum states play a different role from classical ones.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring prepares the state
paragraphs.text: Measuring a full set of compatible quantities at once puts a system into a unique state. The state then changes in a fully determined way under the equations of motion, and a later measurement draws a sample from a predicted probability distribution. So physicists prepare many identical systems, let them evolve, and compare many repeated measurements with the predicted probabilities. Whatever state goes in, repeating the same measurement gives consistent values.

paragraphs.heading: Compatible or not
paragraphs.text: Some later measurements just pin the state down further; these are called compatible. Others change the state and are called incompatible, or complementary. You can measure momentum along the x axis again and again and get the same answer, but measuring position once in between changes later momentum results. This unavoidable disturbance is known as the uncertainty principle.

paragraphs.heading: Pure and mixed
paragraphs.text: Making a complete set of compatible measurements yields what is called a pure state, and any state that is not pure is called mixed. Pure states are usually written as vectors in a Hilbert space. Mixed states are statistical blends of pure states, cannot be written that way, and are usually written as density matrices instead. Experiments rarely produce pure states, so it is mixtures that must be compared with results.

paragraphs.heading: Many ways to write it
paragraphs.text: The same state can be written in different mathematical forms called representations. The position wave function is often the first one beginners meet, and the momentum wave function is an equivalent alternative. Choosing a representation is like choosing a coordinate system: it makes some parts of a problem easier and others harder.
